title: Distance Prediction for Quantum Codes
abstract: The distance of a quantum code is a fundamental metric that dictates its error-correction capability. While quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) families such as Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes offer a promising pathway to low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computing, computing their distance is challenging. Current exact solvers and even search heuristics that provide a distance upper bound suffer from severe computational bottlenecks, restricting the discovery of optimal codes. In this paper, we construct a dataset of BB codes with corresponding distance upper bounds obtained through high-budget heuristic searches. We introduce BB-Net, an attention-based neural network architecture for predicting the distance of BB codes. It achieves 96.39% accuracy on the reference distances in the test set, compared with 94.86% for state-of-the-art heuristics with a budget of up to $10^{4}$ times more computational runtime. On a subset with certified exact distances, BB-Net achieves 98.94%. By relieving the distance-calculation bottleneck, BB-Net enables faster screening of large code spaces, particularly in ML-driven search pipelines, and thereby can accelerate the discovery of novel quantum error-correcting codes, an important capability for advancing scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing. Our code is publicly available: https://github.com/NadavSc/BBNet
summary: This paper introduces BB-Net, an attention-based neural network designed to predict the minimum distance of quantum error-correcting codes, specifically BB codes. By encoding the code's algebraic structure using polynomial and spectral tokens, BB-Net bypasses the NP-hard computational barrier associated with exact distance calculation. This breakthrough significantly accelerates the screening process, aiding the discovery of novel, high-performance quantum codes.
main_problem: The core challenge is the computationally hard problem of determining the minimum distance ($d$) of quantum error-correcting codes, which dictates their fault-tolerance capability.
main_result: The proposed neural network, BB-Net, achieves high accuracy in predicting code distances with a computational cost up to $10^4$ times lower than state-of-the-art heuristic solvers.
method: The authors developed BB-Net, an attention-based neural network that processes the algebraic structure of Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes by combining polynomial and Tanner-spectral token representations.
model_or_system: The focus is on Quantum Error Correction (QEC) using stabilizer codes, specifically Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes, which are analyzed through their parity-check matrices and algebraic structure.
key_observables: The minimum distance ($d$) of the quantum code, defined as the minimum weight of a nontrivial logical operator.
important_parameters: Code parameters ($\ell, m, n, k$), the computational budget (runtime), and the prediction accuracy (e.g., 96.39% on the test set).
main_assumptions: The method assumes the code structure can be effectively tokenized into local (polynomial) and global (spectral) representations, and that ML prediction can reliably substitute for exact, intractable computation.
figures_summary: Figures compare distance estimation methods, showing the massive runtime difference between heuristic searches and BB-Net inference. Ablation studies (Figure 5) validate the necessity of the combined polynomial and spectral encoding branches.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the computational bottleneck of distance finding for QEC codes. It then details the novel BB-Net architecture, which tokenizes the code structure using polynomial and spectral encoders. Finally, it presents empirical results demonstrating the superior speed and accuracy of the ML prediction approach.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical bottleneck in the search for better quantum error-correcting codes, which is foundational for building scalable quantum computers.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Distance estimation for bivariate bicycle codes through two approaches: computationally intensive heuristic search and orders of magnitude more efficient inference using BB-Net. Numbers refer to a full benchmark evaluation.

Figure 2: BB-Net architecture. A BB code is processed by two encoders; The polynomial encoder applies self-attention to monomial tokens and is conditioned on the code parameters through FiLM layers. In parallel, the Tanner spectral encoder processes Fourier-character tokens using attention as well. Each branch produces a code latent representation, which is combined through a learned gated residual connection. The fused representation then passed to a classification head.

Figure 3: BB-Net tokenization and embedding. A BB code specified by sparse polynomials A and B is mapped to two complementary representations: (i) polynomial tokens encode monomial supports on Zℓ× Zm with the type (A,B) indicator as a one-hot vector and the first eight Fourier harmonics, represented by sine and cosine components along each lattice dimension, yielding a 32-dimensional positional representation. (ii) Tanner spectral tokens encode the responses of the full polynomials at each group character χ using 18-dimensional character features. Learned CLS tokens are used as latent vector aggregators for the downstream classification task.

Figure 4: The x-axis denotes the minimum distance threshold t, and the y-axis reports the accuracy computed over codes whose distance satisfies d ≥t. Thus, moving to the right restricts the evalua- tion to increasingly high-distance codes. This was examined on three subsets: the whole benchmark, certified exact distances, and upper bound, unresolved distances.

Figure 5: Bold curves denote the best configuration, including augmentation, shift canonicalisation, and FiLM conditioning; lighter curves show the corresponding model with the component named in each panel removed.
